identity.title: Chest pain radiating to both arms (or right arm/shoulder), with diaphoresis

technique.how: Ask the patient to point to where the pain goes and specifically whether it travels into the right arm, the left arm, both arms, or the shoulders; ask separately about sweating at onset (and look for it). Record radiation to each side, since right-arm and bilateral radiation carry more weight than left-arm radiation alone.
technique.prerequisites: Patient able to describe symptoms; observe for diaphoresis rather than relying solely on report.

interpretation.positive_finding: Radiation to both arms is specific (96%) for ACS with LR ~2.6 in the 2015 RCE and up to 7.1 for MI in the 1998 RCE; right-arm/shoulder radiation and observed sweating also raise the probability (sweating pooled LR+ 2.9).
interpretation.negative_finding: Absence of arm radiation has little value - most ACS patients have no bilateral radiation (low sensitivity), and left-arm radiation alone is nearly uninformative.
interpretation.pitfalls: Left-arm radiation is the 'classic' feature yet barely changes probability; LRs are modest and never replace ECG and troponin; estimates vary with reference standard (MI vs any ACS) and era.
interpretation.changes_what: Positive: increases ACS probability - fast-track ECG/troponin and heighten suspicion even with a normal initial ECG. Negative: no change; proceed with the standard workup.

estimates.target_condition: Acute coronary syndrome (final hospital diagnosis or cardiovascular event within 6 weeks)
estimates.population: ED patients with symptoms suggesting ACS; prospective studies pooled in the RCE (58 studies)
estimates.reference_standard: Final hospital diagnosis of ACS or cardiovascular event within 6 weeks
estimates.quote: pain radiation to both arms (specificity, 96%; LR, 2.6 [95% CI, 1.8-3.7])
estimates.location: Abstract, Results (PubMed abstract; full text/tables not accessible)

estimates.population: Patients with acute chest pain in studies pooled by the 1998 RCE
estimates.reference_standard: Clinical diagnosis of MI (ECG/enzymes per included studies)
estimates.quote: chest pain radiating to both the left and right arm simultaneously (LR, 7.1)
estimates.location: Abstract, Results (PubMed abstract; full text not accessible)

estimates.target_condition: Acute myocardial infarction (WHO criteria) - radiation to shoulder or both arms
estimates.population: 893 consecutive patients with acute, undifferentiated chest pain at a UK ED chest pain unit (AMI 3.8%)
estimates.reference_standard: WHO criteria for AMI with 6-month follow-up
estimates.quote: pain radiating to the shoulder or both arms (LR = 4.07)

estimates.population: Non-selected patients (16 of 28 included studies; primary care and ED populations pooled)
estimates.quote: Sweating had the highest pooled positive likelihood ratio (LR+), namely 2.92 (95% CI = 1.97 to 4.23) for acute myocardial infarction

sources.citation: Fanaroff AC, Rymer JA, Goldstein SA, Simel DL, Newby LK. Does This Patient With Chest Pain Have Acute Coronary Syndrome? The Rational Clinical Examination Systematic Review. JAMA. 2015;314(18):1955-1965.
Panju AA, Hemmelgarn BR, Guyatt GH, Simel DL. The rational clinical examination. Is this patient having a myocardial infarction? JAMA. 1998;280(14):1256-1263.
Goodacre S, Locker T, Morris F, Campbell S. How useful are clinical features in the diagnosis of acute, undifferentiated chest pain? Acad Emerg Med. 2002;9(3):203-208.

Bruyninckx R, Aertgeerts B, Bruyninckx P, Buntinx F. Signs and symptoms in diagnosing acute myocardial infarction and acute coronary syndrome: a diagnostic meta-analysis. Br J Gen Pract. 2008;58(547):105-111.
Body R, Carley S, Wibberley C, McDowell G, Ferguson J, Mackway-Jones K. The value of symptoms and signs in the emergent diagnosis of acute coronary syndromes. Resuscitation. 2010;81(3):281-286.

safety_scope.do_not_use_when: Do not use absence of arm radiation or of sweating to lower suspicion of ACS; do not apply the LRs to patients whose pain is clearly traumatic or reproducible on palpation without also completing the ECG/troponin pathway.
safety_scope.escalation_warning: Bilateral arm radiation with diaphoresis in an acutely unwell patient is high-risk for MI - immediate 12-lead ECG, troponin, aspirin and ACS pathway; consider aortic dissection if pain is tearing or pulses/BP are asymmetric.
safety_scope.interobserver_note: Reliability of eliciting radiation pattern not reported in the RCEs; wording of the question (both arms vs shoulders) changes the estimate, as shown by the spread of LRs (2.6-7.1).

extraction_notes: Fanaroff 2015 abstract supplies specificity and LR with CI but not sensitivity, and the full text/tables are not accessible (no PMC), so sensitivity is null and status is partially_quantified. Panju 1998 (LR 7.1, MI as target; older era) and Goodacre 2002 (LR 4.07, 'shoulder or both arms') are kept as separate entries because target condition, era and question wording differ - not averaged. Body 2010 (ED, n=796) reports adjusted ORs (right arm 2.23, both arms 2.69, sweating observed 5.18), not LRs, so it is cited without numeric entry. Diaphoresis entered as a separate component from Bruyninckx 2008 pooled LR+ 2.92; Goodacre 2002 found diaphoresis not predictive, illustrating heterogeneity.
